title: Genet skull
content:
title: Genet skull
scientific name: Genetta tigrina
located: Redpath Museum RM 660
information: 
What does a genet eat? The genet has a dentition typical of small- to medium-sized carnivorous mammals, but its diet is not just restricted to small rodents and birds. Insects, spiders, scorpions, leaves and even grass have been found in its stomach!
Is the genet active by day or night?  The genet is a nocturnal animal which spends most of its daytime resting in trees. At night, it hunts and feeds on the ground.
Which genet species is it?  This skull was originally referred to the Cape genet (Genetta tigrina) species when it was collected more than 100 years ago. Since then, more research on the group's biology has split this species into several more, so we're not sure which of the new species the skull belongs to now.
What are the genet’s closest evolutionary relatives?  The genet is a carnivoran mammal belonging to Family Viverridae. Hyaenas and mongooses are among this group's closest evolutionary relatives.

What did the ibis mean to ancient Egyptians?  The sacred ibis represents Thoth, the god of wisdom and healing. 
What is this amulet made of?  This amulet is made of steatite, a mineral occasionally nicknamed ‘soapstone’. Today, steatite is used to make products ranging from floor tiles or wood stove covers due to its ability to retain heat.

Why is this falcon statuette painted?  The polychrome patterns of this wooden statuette are a reference to Horus, the falcon-headed god of the sky.
What else can the design of this statuette tell us?  The name Horus is derived from the ancient Egyptian Horou, which means "the  distant" in reference to the flight of the falcon high in the sky.

title: Lion skull
content:
title: Lion skull
scientific name: Panthera leo
located: Redpath Museum
RM 7156
information: 
Top of the food chain  Even if you had never watched a lion feed, you would guess immediately from this skull that this is a meat-eater. Its tooth row bears a clear distinction between incisors, massive canines, and sharp molars for slicing meat called carnassials. 
What place did lions have in ancient Egyptian culture?  A very wide temporal fenestra behind the eyes indicates large jaw muscles which enable high bite forces necessary to catch large prey. 
Why can’t we find lions in Egypt anymore?  During Antiquity, lions ranged across all savannas and semi-arid regions of Africa, including the Mediterranean coastline. This geographical distribution, combined with their awe-inspiring appearance, explains their predominance in several mythologies around the Mediterranean and the Middle East, from Greece to Egypt and Babylon. In Ancient Egypt, the goddess Sekhmet of war and protection was incarnated as a lioness.

Who is Osiris? Osiris is such an important god in the Ancient Egyptian pantheon that he is considered to have invented agriculture and religion in that mythology. Osiris is a funerary god who is the judge of souls that reach the afterlife.
What is this statuette made of?  This statuette is made of bronze and was donated to the Redpath Museum by the Natural History Society of Montreal.

title: Dog skull
content:
title: Dog skull
scientific name: Canis familiaris
located: Redpath Museum
RM 7295
information: 
Humans' best friend...  Millennia of artificial selection by friendly humans on some wolf groups have led to the evolution of the dog. As humans selected for certain traits, dogs now display a few anatomical differences compared to wolves, such as a steeper forehead and a shorter snout depending on the breed.  
…Even into the afterlife  Dogs were common pets in Ancient Egypt and were often mummified to accompany their masters after they died. Other dogs were sacrificed in massive necropolises as votive offerings to Anubis, one of the main gods of death of that civilization.  
When were dogs first domesticated in Egypt? The oldest dog bones found there are from the fifth millennium BC, long before the first pharaonic empire rose in the Nile Valley. This is not surprising since dogs were domesticated by humans many thousands of years before that, perhaps even before the first sedentary societies.

title: Young hippo skull
content:
title: Young hippo skull
scientific name: Hippopotamus amphibius
located: Redpath Museum
RM 5092
information: 
How old was this hippo?  We know that this hippo was not fully grown because (1) this skull is not at full size; (2) the molars at the back of its lower jaw are not erupted yet; (3) the fusion of the two dentaries (lower jaw bones) is incomplete.
Why are the eyes and nostrils right on top of the skull?  Hippos stay cool in Africa’s tropical climate by spending most of their time in water. Having their nostrils on top of their head allows them to keep breathing while bathing!  
Do hippos eat plants or meat?  This skull shows us that hippos are herbivores because their molars and premolars are perfect for grinding grasses and aquatic plants. However, their sharp canines betray how dangerous they can be to other hippos or unfortunate humans who intrude on their patch of freshwater.   
What place did hippos have in ancient Egyptian culture?  Hippos were admired, but also feared, by ancient Egyptians. They incarnated around 4 deities of life and fertility, but they were also prime trophies for pharaohs to hunt to display their power. Hunting may have had a role in driving hippos to extinction in Egypt, but habitat loss caused by agriculture and desertification in the Nile Valley likely contributed as well.

title: Baboon skull
content:
title: Baboon skull
scientific name: Papio sp.
located: Redpath Museum
RM 2392
information: 
A very familiar tooth set  The baboon’s teeth are very similar to those of humans, except for large canines used for self-defence. This dentition overall suggests that baboons were omnivorous, as shown by observing them feeding occasionally on small animals in the wild.  
Can we know which baboon species it is? This skull doesn’t allow us to identify the exact species of baboon it belongs to. However, it is likely to be an olive baboon (Papio anubis). This is by far the most common baboon species in Africa, and ranges from East to West between the Sahara Desert and the equatorial forest. 
However, it is likely to be an olive baboon (Papio anubis). This is by far the most 
common baboon species in Africa, with a range spanning the entire continent from East to West between the Sahara Desert and the equatorial forest.
Is this baboon male or female? This skull already looks very elongated and dog-like compared to most monkey skulls. It belongs to a female baboon because male baboons have even more extreme features which reflect their social status as guardians of their respective groups against predators and adversaries.
A good friend in Ancient Egypt  Baboons were among the most common animals to be mummified as pets, alongside dogs. Of all the pets humans ever had throughout history, it is interesting to note that baboons may be among those with the closest evolutionary link to their owners.

title: Warthog skull
content:
title: Warthog skull
scientific name: Phacochoerus africanus
located: Redpath Museum
RM 5089
information: 
Where does the name 'warthog' come from? The name ‘warthog’ comes from masses of thickened skin called ‘warts’. These protect the jaws, eyes and muzzle of this iconic African animal which arguably reached worldwide fame in The Lion King.  
Why do warthogs have such large tusks? The warthog’s tusks are used during fights among their own kind. Competing warthogs often interrupt their ‘tusk-wrestling’ by thumping each other’s heads, which can result in fractures and even death. The ‘warts’ have evolved over generations as protection from such assaults.  
What do warthogs eat? Warthogs mostly eat leaves and grasses but occasionally eat fallen fruits and small animals. Wear traces indicate where the tusks of the upper and lower jaws frequently rub each other during feeding.  
Weird molars The last molars of the warthog’s tooth row are longer and deeper than the other molars. This ensures that at least one of the teeth they use for masticating tough plant material is durable enough.

title: Falcon mummy
content:
title: Falcon mummy
scientific name: Falco tinnunculus (likely)
located: Redpath Museum
RM 5731
information: 
Can we tell which falcon species this is from the mummy? The falcon species in this 
mummy was identified by 
examining the pattern of the scleral ossicles which form a ring around the orbit. This pattern varies slightly between closely related bird species.
A popular bird for mummies The falcon is one of the 
most commonly found birds in the votive animal mummy record of ancient Egypt. This is likely because many ancient Egyptian gods were depicted with falcon heads, notably Ra and Horus (both gods of the sun and sky). 
Mystery missing bandages Some bandages are missing 
around the tomial tooth (the bump near the tip of the beak). We don’t know whether that was due to erroneous handling of the mummy before its burial, decomposition in the ground after burial, or both. 
Why does part of the skull cover the falcon's eye? The front of the falcon's eyes is partially covered by a narrow strap-like bone. This bone is the lacrymal, and it likely acts as a sunshade for the falcon as it hunts for prey in the air, often under intense sunlight.
The perching digit The first digit of each foot (named 
hallux in birds) is so extended that it looks as if the falcon is perched inside the bandages.

title: Falcon mummy
content:
title: Falcon mummy
scientific name: Falco tinnunculus (likely)
located: Redpath Museum
RM 2726.2
information: 
Can we tell which falcon species this is from the mummy? The falcon species in this mummy was 
identified as the common kestrel by examining the pattern of the scleral ossicles which form a ring around the orbit. This pattern varies slightly between closely related bird species.
How was this falcon sacrificed? The falcon’s head is positioned over its left 
shoulder, with its right shoulder standing slightly outward. This suggests that it died by neck wringing, which is very plausible given that this animal was sacrificed to produce a mummy. 
How did this mummy reach the Redpath Museum? We know that this mummy was donated to the 
Natural History Society of Montreal’s collections by James Ferrier, who likely acquired it during a trip to Egypt in 1859. However, there don’t exist any documents to confirm that. 
How old is this mummy? We know that this mummy was produced around 
15 BC (2 sigma range 52 BC to AD 24) thanks to Carbon 14 dating performed on a piece of fabric that fell off the bundle as it was being transported for CT scanning. Just an example of an initial accident with a happy ending!

title: Ibis mummy
content:
title: Ibis mummy
scientific name: Unknown
located: Redpath Museum
RM 2727.1
information: 
Was this ibis already hatched? We don’t know yet whether this
 ibis was hatched from its egg or when it was mummified. Its fetal position suggests it never hatched. One way in which we could 
determine its growth stage is to examine its vertebrae to assess the degree of fusion between each neural arch and its corresponding centrum. 
What was the role of ibises in ancient Egyptian culture? While the bill of adult ibises is 
recurved, that of juveniles is straight, as in most birds. Why? 
Do we know exactly where this mummy was made? The ibis was a popular bird in 
the votive mummy industry because it is the animal that represented Thoth, god of the Moon, wisdom, knowledge and writing. Adult ibises are much more similar to the depictions of Thoth, and they were also mummified, like this specimen from the British Museum.

title: Ibis mummy?
content:
title: Ibis mummy?
scientific name: nan
located: Redpath Museum
RM 2727.2
information: 
What is inside this bundle? A CT scan revealed that this bundle was 
only filled with rags and that nothing was actually embalmed inside! This is an example of a ‘pseudo-mummy’. Considering that it looks so similar to a real ibis mummy, it may well have been a key component of one of the oldest documented scams in human history!  
Real or fake? In a story published in the National Geographic magazine in 2008, zooarcheologist Salima Ikram notes a trend that might not be so surprising to a 21st-century human: the more attractive the bundle, the more likely it is to contain a fake mummy!  
The real ibis mummy and the fake mummy together present an exception to this rule: the wrapping of the real mummy features a beautiful artistic depiction of an ibis, while that of the fake mummy has no decoration at all. 
Do we know exactly where this mummy was made? We are certain that this pseudo-
mummy was purchased by James Ferrier in Thebes alongside the real ibis mummy. However, we don’t know whether it was really made in Thebes despite this town being one of the Nile valley’s major falcon and ibis necropolises. 
How old is this mummy? We know that this mummy 
was produced around 278 BC (2 sigma range 295 to 208 BC) thanks to Carbon 14 dating. The archeological record suggests that traditional animal cults became more widespread relatively late in ancient Egyptian history (i.e., after roughly 700 BC), perhaps as a reaction to increasing Greek and Roman influence.

title: Cat mummy
content:
title: Cat mummy
scientific name: Felis catus
located: Redpath Museum
RM 2728.1
information: 
How were the cat's soft internal organs removed to make it a mummy? During the embalming process, internal head organs such as the brain were normally removed from the skull through the nasal cavity. In the case of this cat mummy, the brain was removed through the Foramen magnum, the hole at the base of the spinal cord.  
What role did cats have in ancient Egyptian culture? The cat represented the incarnation of Bastet, goddess of protection. Bastet was considered a gentler equivalent to the lioness goddess Sekhmet 
The shifting appreciation of cat mummies Thousands of cats were buried in Istabl Antar, 
the first animal mummy necropolis to be found in modern Egypt in 1888. However, the scientific value of animal mummies was underappreciated back then relative to human remains. As a result, several animal mummies were sold either as curiosities to tourists, or as bulk fertilizer. For instance, one haul of around 180,000 mummies weighing 17,000 kg in total was shipped to Liverpool to fertilize Britain’s agricultural fields. 
Was this cat wild or domesticated? This cat was probably 
domesticated, but you can see a wild African cat elsewhere in the virtual museum.
